papers.title: Physics‐Grounded Rapid Grasp Pose Synthesis for Novel Objects
papers.authors: Xiao Hu, Yang Ye
papers.abstract: Robotic grasping models trained on large‐scale datasets perform well on common objects but often fail on out‐of‐distribution (OOD) objects or nonstandard grippers because of dataset bias and poor physical grounding. To address this, an efficient framework is proposed for fine‐tuning grasping models on novel objects. High‐quality 3D object meshes are reconstructed using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), grasp candidates are generated rapidly by a sampling‐based scheme that sweeps a fixed set of gripper orientations over the reconstructed surface and scores them by force closure, and physics‐based dynamic filtering discards unstable grasps. In a randomized simulation benchmark of 25 objects, including six held‐out objects, fine‐tuning with the proposed labels raises the top‐1 grasp success rate from 62% to 91% (2500 trials per method). In real‐robot experiments on nine objects (135 trials per method), the success rate increases from 29.6% to 73.3%. Generating 6500 grasp labels takes about 2.2 h, compared with about 13 h for an antipodal sampling pipeline. The framework provides a scalable label generation pipeline and a physics‐grounded filtering mechanism that improves real‐world grasping robustness. The reliability of simulation‐based filtering, the sim‐to‐real gap, and the simulation setup effort are discussed as limitations.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
papers.authors: Jungjin Lee, Se Jin Kim, Sung Kwon On, Insoon Yang
papers.abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

papers.title: PSK: A Matrix-Free Single-Loop Method for K-Level Physics-Based Control
papers.authors: Zherong Pan
papers.abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over $K$ steps as $K$-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min--max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop $K$-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an $ε$-stationary control in $O(ε^{-3})$ iterations, with a $K$-independent exponent but a $K$-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz--John, and PSK keeps the $O(ε^{-3})$ complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $ε$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $Ω(ε^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/ε$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.

papers.title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
papers.authors: Yinghao Li, WeiHsien Lee, Zeyu Zhang, Canyang Zhao, Ke Fang, Xing Li, Bing Liu
papers.abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

papers.title: Multimodal Haptic Display Integrating Texture, Softness, and Thermal Rendering for Active Touch
papers.authors: Haewon Jeong, Khoa Lanh, Paulina Gallego Perez, Yasemin Vardar
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Touch allows humans to perceive fundamental cues, such as roughness, friction, softness, and temperature, that define how surfaces feel. Yet these sensations remain largely absent from digital interactions. Here, we present SensaSurf, a unified haptic display that delivers the four primary tactile modalities during active fingertip exploration. SensaSurf combines electrovibration for roughness and friction, a pneumatically actuated origami joint for stiffness, and a temperature‐controlled origami bellows for thermal and contact area modulation, enabling independent control of lateral force, effective stiffness, contact area, and temperature across perceptually relevant ranges. A user study showed that these capabilities produce distinct multimodal sensations spanning major dimensions of touch. To our knowledge, SensaSurf is the first surface‐based haptic display to integrate all primary tactile modalities during active bare‐finger interaction, opening opportunities to study multisensory perception and to advance multimodal tactile surface rendering in digital environments.

papers.title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Zequan Zeng, Junqin Yang, Kai Wang
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.

papers.title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
papers.authors: Nathalia Gomez, Haig Shamlian, Omar Khan, Tiffany D. Do
papers.abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.

papers.title: Leaning Over to Reach Far-Away Objects
papers.authors: Allen Devaraj, William Xie, Nikolaus Correll
papers.abstract: We study supported reaching to extend a humanoid robot's workspace by bracing against the environment for stabilization using a straightforward yet capable whole-body model predictive control (MPC) approach, exclusively with local sensing and fiducial markers. While typical solutions for whole body humanoid control aim at avoiding or accommodating contact, contact is explicitly required to reach objects placed on surfaces far out of normal reach. We employ sampling-based MPC for whole-body leaning, bracing, reaching, and recovery on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid. The controller runs in real-time at 34 Hz on a laptop, transfers sim-to-real, extends reach by about 50 cm beyond the unbraced standing workspace, and sustains the loaded posture for over four minutes, before pose estimation drifts. The controller reaches the commanded target in 89% of trials and completes the full reach-and-recovery cycle in 81%, across 54 trials spanning six targets and three table heights. We further characterize why such a small real-time sampling budget is sufficient, finding that temporal persistence of sampled actions and exploration scale strongly govern success, while CEM provides the widest operating region over planning rate and model mismatch. These results establish a real-world baseline for online, contact-rich humanoid manipulation. Code, videos, and full hardware details are available at https://h12leaner.github.io/

papers.title: Intraoperative technology in skull base and vascular neurosurgery: a two-stage cross-sectional national survey
papers.authors: Ahmad M. S. Ali, JOHN GERRARD HANRAHAN, Carole L. Turner, Andrew Folusho Alalade, Alexandros Boukas, Dimitris Paraskevopolos, Puneet Plaha, Hani Joseph Marcus
papers.abstract: Skull base and vascular neurosurgery rely on diverse intraoperative technologies, but contemporary data describing how frequently they are used at the level of individual operations are limited. On behalf of the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS) MedTech Committee, we aimed to establish a dated descriptive baseline of reported technology use across three operative paradigms. We conducted a two-stage cross-sectional survey of neurosurgeons in the UK and Ireland via the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS). Six MedTech Committee members compiled a pragmatic technology list. Respondents reported frequency of use for three exemplar procedures: transsphenoidal pituitary adenoma, retrosigmoid vestibular schwannoma, and pterional aneurysm surgery. Use was recorded on a four-point ordinal scale and analysed descriptively, with Kendall's tau-b used to explore the relationship between experience and reported use. Twenty-four responses from 20 of the 32 adult or mixed adult-paediatric UK units were analysed (11 units per index procedure). Reported use was strongly procedure specific. Neuronavigation was used always or almost always by 8/12 transsphenoidal respondents but infrequently elsewhere. Endoscopy had displaced microscopy in transsphenoidal surgery, whereas microscopy was used always or almost always by all retrosigmoid and pterional respondents. Indocyanine green and micro-Doppler were routine for aneurysms. Neurophysiological monitoring was universal for vestibular schwannoma but evenly divided for aneurysms. Exoscopes, intraoperative MRI and robotics were used infrequently or not at all; augmented reality was reported by 5/13 pterional respondents. No association was found between experience and reported use, though this was underpowered. Reported intraoperative technology use is strongly shaped by operative paradigm, with established technologies clustering around recurring procedural needs. Newer technologies were used infrequently. Because availability was not recorded, non-use cannot be distinguished from lack of access. These data provide a dated baseline against which future change can be assessed.

papers.title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
papers.authors: Matthias Jammot, Pembe Gizem Özdil
papers.abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

papers.title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
papers.authors: Gaytri Jena, Kapil Wanaskar, Aman Chadha, Vasu Sharma, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das
papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.

papers.title: Few-Shot Visual Concept Extraction for Steering Diffusion Transformers
papers.authors: Nabyl Quignon, Antitza Dantcheva
papers.abstract: Image steering aims to provide fine-grained control over concepts in generated images, enabling targeted and continuous manipulation without broadly altering the generation process. Recent steering methods for diffusion models primarily focus on the text-conditioning space or rely on costly auxiliary training. Deviating from that, we here propose a novel steering approach that extracts visual concept directions directly from the image-side activations of Diffusion Transformers. Specifically, we showcase few-shot concept extraction in the activation space using a simple difference-of-means estimator over intermediate residuals. We observe (a) scene-level concepts such as lighting, weather, and style are distributed across image tokens, as well as (b) local concepts such as object colors, textures, materials, and facial attributes are concentrated in specific regions. Towards controlling both concepts, we introduce a new unified training-free framework that uses global difference-of-means for (a) distributed concepts and masked difference-of-means for (b) local concepts, preventing local signals from being diluted by global averaging. Notably, using only a handful of positive and negative prompt pairs, our method identifies and extracts reusable concept directions that can be injected at inference for continuous steering. Quantitatively, our method outperforms text-encoder steering and training-free activation-editing baselines, as well as is competitive with specialized editing models. Our results suggest that as concept directions can be applied at patch level, our method enables precise targeted and compositional steering, manipulating multiple concepts in the same image.

papers.title: Ego2Sim2Humanoid: Agentic Real-to-Sim for Learning Loco-Manipulation VLAs without Robot Demonstrations
papers.authors: Chen Liu, Nikolaus Correll
papers.abstract: Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware. Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible contacts. \method{} converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams, completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards, completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot's onboard camera along the optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset, without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks autonomously on a Unitree G1. papers.title: Distributed Shaping of Robot Swarms Through Spatial Moments of Arbitrary Order
papers.authors: Jin Chen, Hector Garcia de Marina
papers.abstract: This paper shapes a swarm into a target pattern, such as a figure taken from an image, by controlling its spatial moments. The image is sampled into a reference configuration whose centroid and covariance set the position and principal spreads of the formation, while its higher-order moments, expressed in covariance-normalized (whitened) coordinates, encode the remaining shape. In contrast with geometric formation control, which prescribes distances, bearings, or relative positions between specific agents, this specification concerns the swarm as a whole and assigns no agent to a particular place. The key mechanism is orthogonalization in the swarm's own empirical inner product: projecting negative-gradient velocities onto the complement of low-degree polynomials sampled at the agents makes every higher-order correction preserve all lower-order moments exactly. The resulting hierarchical controller has lower triangular error dynamics and converges locally exponentially for any positive gains, so orders can be added without undoing those already achieved. A joint alternative regulates the higher moments together through a regularized Gauss--Newton step while preserving the centroid and covariance dynamics. We give bounds on the number of agents and sufficient conditions for regularity. Both controllers admit a distributed implementation that uses only relative positions and neighbor communication and retains local exponential convergence when estimation is sufficiently fast. In a distributed simulation on a sparse graph, 350 agents form an airplane from an unstructured swarm through moments up to order ten; the hierarchy reaches the full specification, while the joint law approaches it with smaller velocities.

papers.title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
papers.authors: Srikar Babu Gadipudi, Somayeh Sojoudi, Claire J. Tomlin
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.

papers.title: Depth-Aware Path Planning and Collision Avoidance for Robotic Nursing Assistants Using Real-Time 3D Vision
papers.authors: Peeyush Thakur, Dharmendra Sharma, Archit Sharma, Sandeep Gupta, Anuj Nandanwar, Laxmidhar Behera
papers.abstract: This paper presents a depth-aware path planning and collision avoidance framework for the safe navigation of robotic nursing assistants in cluttered environments with low-height obstacles. Conventional LiDAR-based navigation systems, while accurate for mapping and localization, fail to detect transparent or low-height obstacles, whereas vision-based systems are prone to noise and occlusion. The proposed framework integrates RGB-D depth sensing, rule-based obstacle avoidance, and the NavfnROS global path planner to drive the robot from an initial point to a goal point. The proposed approach is implemented on the Husky A200 robot, equipped with a Kinova Gen3 arm, to form a complete setup for a robotic nursing assistant. This system features a multi-layer architecture for global planning, perception fusion, and real-time control in the ROS-Gazebo environment. Experimental evaluations in a simulated cluttered environment demonstrate up to 40\% higher success rate and 35\% improvement in minimum clearance compared with single-sensor baselines. Furthermore, real-world experimental results validate the proposed approach as a computationally efficient and safety-aware navigation solution for autonomous healthcare robots.

papers.title: DecoEdit: Beyond Flat Control for 3D-Aware Unified Image Editing
papers.authors: Xiaotang Gai, Jinbo Xing, Zijie Meng, Jiayi Yi, Jimin Xiao, Yixuan Qian, Yu Liu, Chaojie Mao, et al.
papers.abstract: While recent advances in multimodal image editing have achieved impressive results, current frameworks remain largely confined to ``flat" 2D controls (e.g., text prompts, bounding boxes, or masks). Precise 3D-aware geometric manipulation -- such as coordinating an object's location, physical scale, and 3D orientation while strictly preserving its fine-grained identity -- remains an elusive challenge, typically suffering from severe detail degradation or requiring expensive per-instance fine-tuning. In this paper, we present DecoEdit, an all-in-one image editing framework that goes beyond flat control by seamlessly integrating 1D textual, 2D spatial, and 3D volumetric inputs under a unified architecture. First, to power this unified model, we establish a data curation pipeline and curate a large-scale dataset, namely DecoDataset, containing 1.6 million samples, encompassing diverse multi-dimensional (1D/2D/3D) tasks and their complex compositions. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive image editing benchmark named DecoBench to systematically evaluate multi-task editing performance. Finally, to address the fundamental trade-off between complex spatial transformations and identity preservation, we propose a novel decoupled pipeline: DecoEdit factorizes the editing process by utilizing structural guidance from SAM-3D to anchor the target geometry, scale, and spatial orientation, while concurrently leveraging a detail-preservation path to lock in high-fidelity textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoEdit achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, on the challenging 3D spatial pose and orientation control tasks, DecoEdit significantly outperforms leading closed-source models such as Seedream 5.0 in both geometric accuracy and identity consistency.

papers.title: Cooperative Gradient Estimation for Multi-Robot Source Seeking with Heteroskedastic Measurements
papers.authors: Alessandro Renzaglia, Lara Briñón-Arranz
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for localizing the source of a three-dimensional scalar field using a team of heterogeneous cooperative mobile robots. Each robot measures the field intensity at its location and shares the information within the team. Measurement noise is explicitly considered, and heterogeneity arises from robot-dependent sensing accuracies, leading to heteroskedastic data. The proposed framework combines a weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellation-based formation strategy, defined on a spherical surface and parameterized by sensor noise variances, with a Weighted Least Squares estimator to compute the field gradient at the formation center. By explicitly accounting for sensor heterogeneity in both formation design and estimation, the method achieves robust gradient estimation under noisy measurements. In particular, we show analytically that this construction is nearly optimal. The covariance of the gradient estimate is derived in closed form, providing a lower bound on the attainable estimation variance for any formation on the sphere, and the proposed tessellation is shown to asymptotically satisfy the conditions under which this bound is attained. The estimated gradient is then exploited within a gradient-ascent strategy to guide the team toward the source location. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to alternative strategies and highlight its intrinsic ability to reconfigure online in response to robot failures, thereby enhancing its adaptability.

papers.title: Comparing Haptic Feedback Across Hand Tracking and Controllers in VR Object Interaction Tasks
papers.authors: Natalia Ocampo, J. Felipe Gonzalez, Robert J. Teather, Kiyoshi Kiyokawa
papers.abstract: Hand tracking offers natural VR interaction but lacks controllers’ inherent tactile feedback, while haptic feedback across input methods remains understudied. We conducted a participant study comparing vibration, impulse, and no feedback in hand- and controller-based VR interaction across grasp-, pinch-, and tap-like gestures assessing performance, workload, and preference. A custom glove and controller-mounted device provided both feedback types, aiming for consistency across input modalities. Controllers were faster for grasp and pinch, whereas hand tracking was more accurate for pinch and preferred overall. Haptics had limited performance effects, although impulse reduced grasp accuracy with controllers. Participants preferred vibration and impulse over no haptic feedback, favouring vibration overall. Our findings reveal a more nuanced relationship between haptic feedback, input device, and interaction context than suggested by previous work.

papers.title: Collision detection in polishing robots based on self-supervised learning
papers.authors: Yan Xing, Fengnan Zhang, Dajiang Liu, Demin Mu
papers.abstract: Polishing robots are widely used in industrial surface-finishing tasks, but collision detection remains challenging because labeled collision data are costly and potentially hazardous to collect. This paper proposes a self-supervised collision-detection framework that learns temporal representations from unlabeled robot interaction data without requiring collision labels during pre-training. A modality-specific dual-encoder architecture based on Gated Recurrent Units separately models joint motion and current-related signals, while intra-modal contrastive objectives and cross-modal alignment capture temporal consistency and complementary dynamic information. After pre-training, both encoders are frozen and only a lightweight probe classifier is trained for downstream collision detection. Task-oriented signal augmentations are further introduced to improve robustness to polishing-related disturbances. On a highly imbalanced simulation benchmark, the proposed method achieves an Area Under the Precision–Recall Curve (PR-AUC) of \(94.02\%\) , a Best F1-score of \(93.88\%\) , and a Recall of \(94.77\%\) under a false-positive-rate constraint of 0.5% (R@FPR \(\le\) 0.5%), outperforming the compared methods across the four reported metrics. In controlled real-world proof-of-concept experiments on an RM65 robotic arm, few-shot probe adaptation improves window-level Recall from 73.44% to 86.08% and trial-level Recall from 60.00% to 79.20%. These results demonstrate the potential of self-supervised multimodal representation learning for collision detection under polishing-related conditions, while indicating that further validation is needed for practical deployment.

papers.title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
papers.authors: Angelo Moroncelli, Loris Roveda
papers.abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. papers.title: Autonomous navigation of multiple reconfigurable ferrofluid droplet robots in complex environments
papers.authors: Guangming Cui, Xianrui Zhang, Zhenping Yu, Ang Liu, Juntian Qu
papers.abstract: Ferrofluid-based soft robots with extreme deformability have emerged as promising manipulation tools for diverse biomedical applications. Their unique properties to navigate irregular terrains and access otherwise unreachable regions within confined spaces have enabled new opportunities in targeted drug delivery, microfluidic logistics, and lab/organ on-a-chip. However, achieving dynamic motion planning and intelligent behavior for multiple reconfigurable ferrofluid droplet robots (FDRs) is still one of the major challenges yet to be solved. In this paper, we develop a novel framework that integrates dynamic path planning with adaptive motion control for teams of deformable FDRs to autonomously navigate through diverse scenarios involving moving obstacles. We first introduce a distributed magnetic field actuation platform capable of generating a series of local magnetic field sources to enable discrete locomotion and extreme deformation of multiple FDRs. Subsequently, an incremental version of the conflict-based search (CBS) algorithm, called the ICBS, is presented, which aims at finding conflict-free paths for more than one agent (i.e., FDR) and updating the plan according to changes in the environment or missions. To quantitatively describe different behaviors of FDRs and realize adaptive morphology transition, an image-guided motion-deformation controller combined with a finite state machine (FSM) is then designed. The physical and actuation constraints associated with the system are also considered for FDRs in close proximity so that they can smoothly traverse the planned waypoints in the form of localized step-by-step. Finally, extensive simulations and experiments are performed under different conditions to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the deployed FDRs are capable of fully automated navigation with adaptive morphology transitions (stretching, splitting, and merging) in various complex environments.

papers.title: Adaptive visual perception and navigation framework for safe indoor mobility of visually impaired users
papers.authors: Thandu Nagaraju, Rathinam Murugeswari
papers.abstract: Indoor mobility for visually impaired people is an essential problem due to dynamic obstacles and inadequate real-time detection systems. Existing solutions have been found lacking in terms of robustness and adaptability. The current research develops a robust adaptive visual perception and navigation system based on obstacle detection and indoor navigation in real time. The system consists of You Only Look Once version 11 (YOLOv11) algorithm for obstacle detection, Multi-Scale Feature Enhancement (MSFE) for better representation of smaller and distant obstacles, a pixel-wise replacement approach through Kernel Density Estimation (Ps-KDE) for pre-processing with illumination variation, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for adaptive decisions in navigation, and Adaptive Coyote-Badger Optimization (ACBO) for learning. The developed indoor high-resolution dataset consists of 23 obstacle classes and was used to train and evaluate the proposed algorithm; the NYU Depth v2 and SUN RGB-D datasets were also utilized for validation. This model has been able to generate 97.52% Mean Average Precision (mAP) and 96.67% Mean Average Recall (mAR) in the customized dataset with an average frame per second of 55.6 FPS, which makes it suitable for mobile applications. For the scale evaluation, distance estimation, camera position, ablation, and real-life tests are carried out to further evaluate each component as well as the entire framework. A mobile application for providing navigation guidance through text to speech has been implemented. This framework shows its effectiveness under different indoor scenarios without depth sensing.

papers.title: AcousticBEV: Acoustic BEV Object Localization for Intelligent Vehicles
papers.authors: Ziang Liu, Shiming Wang, Joseph Adeola, Julian F. P. Kooij
papers.abstract: Modern autonomous driving and driver assistance systems rely predominantly on cameras, radars and LiDARs for environmental perception. However, these modalities face different environmental limitations, including poor illumination for cameras and adverse weather for LiDAR. Acoustic sensing, particularly using microphone arrays, could provide complementary perception capabilities for autonomous driving, but has remained largely underexplored. In this work, we design a horizontally arranged microphone array that functions as the "ears" of a vehicle, enabling localization of nearby moving vehicles in a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation that captures both their relative direction and distance. Using this array, we collect a real-world driving dataset, AcousticScenes, which contains 2,117 static and 2,863 dynamic samples with synchronized spatial acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds and 3D bounding box annotations. Building on this dataset, we propose AcousticBEV, a learning-based method for acoustic BEV object localization, which estimates the center locations of moving traffic participants in BEV from the microphone-array signals, conditioned on the ego vehicle's own speed. Experimental results demonstrate that AcousticBEV outperforms both classical signal-processing baselines and other learning-based methods, achieving F1 scores of $47.7 \pm 1.2$% on "Easy" scenarios and $45.1 \pm 1.4$% on "Difficult" cases. Our findings demonstrate that acoustic signals from a low-cost, vehicle-mounted microphone array can localize nearby moving vehicles in both azimuth and distance.

papers.title: World models: Enabling the next AI revolution
papers.authors: Yann LeCun, Pascale Fung
papers.abstract: What distinguishes a cat that climbs a cabinet and turns a doorknob to exit a room from your favorite large language model (LLM) chatbot or agent?The cat possesses an intuitive understanding of physical laws-gravity, friction, its own body dynamics-and can plan and execute a sequence of actions without explicit instruction or prior training on that specific task.In contrast, an LLM chatbot generates responses token by token, trained on vast symbolic datasets but lacking three abilities: (1) an understanding of the physical world, (2) an ability to predict the consequences of its own actions, (3) an ability to plan a sequence of actions to accomplish a particular task.Future advanced machine intelligence must integrate the cat's embodied reasoning capabilities alongside the linguistic proficiency of current models.This paper argues that scaling token-generative architectures alone will not deliver the next AI revolution.Instead, progress requires a fundamental shift toward world models: Learned internal representations that encode the state of the environment, predict the outcomes of potential actions, and enable planning under explicit objectives and constraints.Contemporary AI systems remain surprisingly limited in the kinds of intelligence that humans and animals demonstrate effortlessly in physical settings (LeCun, 2022).Moreover, this worldmodel paradigm must extend to human-facing agents that comprehend users' knowledge, beliefs, goals, and social contexts (Fung et al., 2025).

papers.title: Whole-Body Contact-Rich Compliant Motion Planning Based on Morphology Representation
papers.authors: Chengjin Wang, Zheng Yan, Yanmin Zhou, Runjie Shen, Bin He
papers.abstract: Robots operating in cluttered environments require whole-body contact-rich motion planning to safely interact with surrounding objects. However, model-based methods struggle with unknown interaction dynamics, while learning-based methods often depend on task-specific demonstrations or rewards. This paper proposes a physics-model-guided motion planning framework that learns task-agnostic whole-body interactions through material-point morphology representation and interaction prediction supervision. The representation encodes distributed body motion and tactile states with consistent body correspondence, accommodating time-varying contact configurations. A tactile-driven interaction planner generates physically informed motion references to supervise MorphoPlanner, an end-to-end network that predicts future whole-body motion morphologies from task goals and current interaction states without task-specific demonstrations or reward design. A dataset of 749 K tactile interaction samples is constructed for training and evaluation. Simulation and real-world dual-arm experiments demonstrate compliant interactions and improved planning performance over representative baselines, achieving 95.5–100% success rates in dense cluttered scenarios. These results demonstrate the potential of morphology-based physical supervision for whole-body interaction planning in unknown environments.

papers.title: Who Is the Agent Talking To? Participant-Aware Role Switching for Embodied Student-Support Dialogue
papers.authors: Iro Samuel, Filip Janik, Ewa Olton, Robert Smales, Harris Spratt, Shea Tait, Md Zia Ullah, Yanchao Yu
papers.abstract: We present RPO-PDT, an embodied conversational agent that adapts its conversational role to the current participant. It acts as a Personal Development Tutor (PDT) when supporting students and as a simulated student when faculty rehearse tutoring strategies. Voluntary closed-set participant verification informs a confidence-controlled role manager: stable enrolled-faculty matches activate the Student role, while enrolled students and unmatched participants use the default PDT role and uncertain observations cause no transition. The system combines Furhat interaction, Rasa orchestration, institutional retrieval, safeguarding, and LLM-based generation. papers.title: When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners
papers.authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Mike Degany, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang, Matyas Szanto
papers.abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.

papers.title: When Does Cross-View Consistency Matter in Multi-View Appearance Augmentation? A Controlled Study for Visuomotor Policies
papers.authors: Zixuan Jiang
papers.abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.

papers.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Wenhan Wu, Linghan Chen, Yudong Gao, Fan Yang, Honglong Chen, Kai Yin, Jiawei Jiang, Chuang Hu
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.

papers.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
papers.authors: Kate Duffy, Elise Penn, Tristan Ballard, August Posch, Thomas J. Vandal
papers.abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

papers.title: Wearable EEG-Based Kansei Monitoring of Cognitive–Emotional States During a Standardized Simulation Task on a Robotic Surgical System: An Exploratory Feasibility Study
papers.authors: Yusuke Watanabe, Susumu Shibasaki, Yasue Mitsukura, Shutaro Hori, Daiki Kimura, Sota Hoshino, Masaya Nakauchi, Tsuyoshi Tanaka
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose This exploratory feasibility study examined whether a wearable electroencephalography (EEG)-based Kansei analyzer could provide continuous time-series cognitive–emotional data during simulation tasks on a robotic surgical system, and characterized preliminary experience-related patterns, action-specific variations, and temporal relationships among EEG-derived Kansei parameters. Methods Twelve surgeons (novice, intermediate, expert; n = 4 per group) performed six repetitions of the Advanced Training in Laparoscopic Suturing (ATLAS) needle handling task on the da Vinci Xi Surgical System while wearing a single-channel EEG-based Kansei analyzer. Five EEG-derived Kansei parameters (Stress, Like, Interest, Concentration, and Calmness) were recorded at 1 Hz. Experience-related patterns, action-specific Stress patterns, lagged relationships among selected parameters, and associations with task score were examined descriptively. Results All 12 surgeons completed all repetitions without signal acquisition failure, missing data, or task interruption. Across 72 trials, higher task scores were associated with lower 95th-percentile Stress Z-scores (ρ = −0.34), including within participants (repeated-measures r = − 0.25), although attenuated after further adjustment. The expert group showed the highest median Stress value but fewer extreme Stress elevations. Median Stress was highest during Manipulation and lowest during Extraction. Lagged Stress–Concentration correlations were small, positive in experts and predominantly negative in intermediates. Conclusions Continuous wearable EEG-based Kansei monitoring was achieved during simulation tasks using a robotic surgical system without interfering with task execution, indicating that intraoperative monitoring is highly feasible. In exploratory analyses, better-performing trials involved fewer excessive transient Stress elevations, even within individual surgeons, supporting further validation of EEG-derived Kansei metrics against established workload and physiological measures.

papers.title: Vision-informed short-horizon prediction for the squeeze flow of soft materials
papers.authors: Soshala Weerathunge, Nick O. Jaensson, Alessandro Saccon, Clemens V. Verhoosel
papers.abstract: Accurate yet computationally efficient models of soft-material deformation are essential for real-time prediction and control in robotic manipulation. Recent advances in machine learning for object detection and image segmentation have made it possible to reliably extract geometric observations from raw RGB data, opening new avenues for vision-based prediction. Building on these advances, this work investigates the feasibility of a vision-informed framework that couples coarse finite element simulations with continuous parameter recalibration to obtain action-responsive models of soft-material flow suitable for model-based planning and control. Leveraging RGB observations of squeeze flow experiments, the framework repeatedly identifies effective viscosity and slip parameters of a Stokes model over short moving windows via Gauss–Newton updates. Synthetic datasets and physical experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves reliable short-horizon predictions of the sample deformation and maintains geometric consistency despite observation noise and partial parameter identifiability.

papers.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
papers.authors: Suvarna Kadam, Soran Parsa
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

papers.title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
papers.authors: Jie Hu, Yu Zheng, Wenzhi Wu, Weixing Feng, Cunlei Cheng, Jiaming Zhang
papers.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.

papers.title: VACO: Vertex-Aligned Decoding for Dense Hand Contact Estimation from a Single Image
papers.authors: Binhong Ye, Jin-Chuan Shi, Tao Liu, Xin Wang, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
papers.abstract: Dense hand contact estimation from a single RGB image is a foundational primitive for dexterous manipulation and 3D interaction analysis. Direct predictors typically decode the entire per-vertex contact map from one shared query, leaving individual vertices ungrounded in the image and smearing contact across adjacent, non-touching surfaces. We present VACO, a vertex-aligned decoder in which each MANO vertex samples local image features at its projected location. A hand-reconstruction backbone, jointly trained for reconstruction and contact, predicts these locations at inference without an auxiliary reconstructor. Training uses noise-perturbed ground-truth projections and end-to-end feature adaptation to improve robustness and contact-sensitive features. A single VACO checkpoint sets a new state of the art on five benchmarks spanning hand-object, hand-human, hand-scene, and bimanual interactions. It improves F1 by +20.7 pp over the strongest prior direct predictor on Hi4D and generalizes to the held-out HOT3D and HOCap, with gains of +5.5 and +2.7 pp. The resulting contact predictions also improve downstream HOI reconstruction.

papers.title: Using probabilistic movement primitives for trajectory prediction in minimally invasive robotic surgery
papers.authors: Konstantinos Katsianis
papers.abstract: This thesis examines the problem of reconstructing and predicting surgical trajectories in a robotic surgery environment.Unlike previous approaches that focus primarily on gesture recognition or prediction of entire surgical procedures, the present work focuses on modeling and predicting individual surgical movements.The JIGSAWS dataset, which includes kinematic data and labeled surgical gestures from users of different experience levels, was used to train and evaluate the proposed models, with an emphasis on the individual surgical gestures that compose the suturing process.Probabilistic Movement Primitives (ProMPs) were chosen as the basic modeling framework, due to their ability to probabilistically represent complex movements, to preserve information about the variability of demonstrations, and to perform trajectory prediction.To address the limitations of conventional ProMPs in terms of translations and rotations, six alternative approaches were developed and evaluated.Of these, Primitives of Derivatives and Primitives of Curvature and Torsion showed the most promising results, allowing the creation of models that are more independent of the position and orientation of the gesture execution.Experimental results showed that the derivative-based approach provides the highest accuracy and stability in trajectory prediction, while the curvature-and-torsion approach demonstrates significant potential for future research.In parallel, probabilistic libraries of surgical gestures were created, capable of representing and predicting the movements of experienced surgeons.Although the proposed framework is designed to model and predict multidimensional trajectories in general, the JIGSAWS dataset was selected as a representative and highly demanding benchmark for training and evaluation.The results demonstrate that Movement Primitive frameworks constitute an effective and interpretable approach for trajectory modeling, establishing a foundation for future applications in robotic surgery, surgeon training, haptic guidance, and intelligent robotic assistance, while remaining applicable to other trajectory prediction problems beyond the surgical domain.

papers.title: User Understanding of Robot Learning Evaluations through Task Success Rates and Beyond
papers.authors: Isaac S. Sheidlower, Jindan Huang, James Staley, Bingyu Wu, Qicong Chen, Reuben M. Aronson, Elaine Schaertl Short
papers.abstract: Robot Foundation Models (RFMs) and related robot learning techniques represent a promising approach to developing general-purpose home robots. Given the broad capabilities of RFMs, users will inevitably ask an RFM-based robot to perform tasks that the RFM was not trained or evaluated on. In these cases, it is crucial that users understand the risks associated with attempting novel tasks due to the relatively high cost of failure. Furthermore, an informed user who understands an RFM’s capabilities will know what situations and tasks the robot can handle. In this paper, we study how non-experts interpret performance information from RFM and similar robot learning evaluations. These evaluations typically report task success rate (TSR) as the primary performance metric. While TSR is intuitive to experts, it is necessary to validate whether novices also use this information as intended. Toward this end, we conducted a study in which users saw real evaluation data, including TSR, failure case descriptions, and videos from multiple published robot learning projects. The results highlight that non-experts use TSR in a manner consistent with expert expectations and highly value other information types, such as failure cases that are not often reported in RFM evaluations. Furthermore, we find that users want access to both real data from previous evaluations of the RFM and estimates from the robot about how well it will do on a novel task.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Embodied Artificial Intelligence with Hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control for Resilient Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems
papers.authors: Babak Rahmani, Fatemeh Afghah
papers.abstract: Abstract Embodied artificial intelligence (Embodied AI) has rapidly emerged as a fundamental paradigm for developing autonomous robotic systems capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting within complex physical environments. Recent advances in foundation models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures have significantly improved high-level semantic reasoning for robotics; however, their deployment in real-world field environments remains limited by distributional shifts, multimodal uncertainty, dynamic environmental changes, and the absence of safety-aware decision-making mechanisms. These challenges become substantially more pronounced in heterogeneous multi-robot systems operating under partial observability and communication constraints. This paper presents an uncertainty-aware embodied AI framework that integrates multimodal perception, shared latent world modelling, predictive uncertainty estimation, online self-supervised representation adaptation, and hierarchical decision-making through hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control (RL-MPC). Unlike conventional embodied AI architectures that execute fixed perception and control pipelines, the proposed framework continuously maintains and updates an internal world representation, enabling adaptive reasoning, uncertainty-aware planning, and safe real-time control. Furthermore, the architecture naturally extends to heterogeneous teams of aerial robots, autonomous ground vehicles, and mobile manipulators through distributed latent representations that support cooperative perception, coordinated task allocation, and resilient autonomous behavior. The proposed framework is evaluated in photorealistic NVIDIA Isaac Sim environments containing randomized terrain geometry, vegetation density, illumination changes, dynamic obstacles, sensor degradation, communication uncertainty, and severe out-of-distribution conditions representative of realistic field robotic deployments. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over vision-based navigation, reinforcement learning, model predictive control, and hybrid RL-MPC baselines. The proposed method achieves approximately 21% higher navigation success, reduces collision frequency by more than 35%, exhibits significantly improved robustness under increasing environmental uncertainty, and maintains stable cooperative performance across heterogeneous multi-robot teams. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-aware embodied world models, continual representation learning, hierarchical VLA-guided decision making, and hybrid learning-control architectures provide a scalable foundation for resilient embodied intelligence and represent a promising direction toward next-generation autonomous robotic systems operating safely and reliably in complex real-world environments.

papers.title: UPPER-LIMB MOTOR RESTORATION AFTER STROKE AT THE LIMIT F091-F095 | A FIVE-FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK | 33 x STARLI STATUS: prospective nonclinical research design, synthetic numerical examples, not an experiment with patients and not an established clinical effect. A LETTER FROM THE RESEARCH GENERATION A hand arriving at its goal is an astonishingly incomplete explanation. The shoulder might rotate, the trunk might lean, the fingers might squeeze too hard, or the robot might do the last crucial part of the movement. A science of upper-limb restoration must tell those worlds apart. This notebook examines the untrained reach, safe grasp, independent digit force, multijoint coordination and novel-object device-off transfer as distinct proposed mechanisms. Its mission is not to declare improvement from synthetic diagrams, but to design measurements that might overturn the claim. The integrated F091-F095 family proposes five distinct causal tests. F091 asks whether trajectory quality remains improved after trunk compensation is measured. F092 challenges a seemingly good grasp by concealing object stiffness and logging release failures. F093 separates independent finger control from total force. F094 dissects shoulder-elbow-wrist synergy and passive joint coupling. F095 tests untrained object manipulation with the device fully switched off. These tests are proposed for an inert mechanical arm and offline synthetic datasets, not a clinical evaluation. Our five-stage parallel spacetime reasoning is an intellectual strategy: lock the origin of the question, formalize candidate relations, allow a rival causal world, discover limits through safe bounded stress, and transfer the contradiction to a future laboratory. The name describes distinct branches of scientific interpretation, not physical travel between timelines. The longer this book survives, the more likely its apparatus will seem primitive. A valuable manuscript should let tomorrow's investigator explain exactly why it became obsolete. FOURTEEN RESEARCH PRELUDES 01 | A reached object is not proof of arm restoration One can move a hand to a target using different mixtures of elbow rotation, shoulder elevation, trunk translation and external actuation. This book therefore treats movement quality and genuine device-off object use as separate inferential claims. The science proposed here is prospective and nonclinical; its synthetic curves represent hypotheses rather than human improvement. A representative unresolved case is shoulder abduction as a compensatory shortcut. papers.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.authors: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo, Fangzhou Zhao, Yilong Zhao, Zekai Li, Xingyang Li, Yuyang Zhao, et al.
papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

papers.title: Towards sustainable weed management: the role of artificial intelligence, sensing, and robotics
papers.authors: Ashish Chaudhary, Swas Kaushal, Het Samir Desai, Navjot Singh, Muskan Jakhar, Devanshi Het Desai, Jaswinder Kaur, Komal Mahajan
papers.abstract: Weeds are a major constraint to crop production worldwide. Overreliance on herbicides has led to environmental concerns, selection of herbicide-resistant weed populations, and reduced agroecosystem resilience. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, along with innovations in remote sensing, robotics, and automation, are shifting weed management from uniform field-scale interventions to site-specific, plant-level decision-making. This review synthesizes current developments in AI-enabled precision weed management, with emphasis on sensing technologies, image-processing workflows, weed detection algorithms, and targeted weed-control systems. We also consider AI-assisted herbicide-response phenotyping, including crop injury, off-target drift, and herbicide-resistance assessment. We discuss commercial and emerging precision weed-management technologies, including targeted herbicide spraying, robotic mechanical weeding, and laser-based weed control. Beyond operational efficiency, we provide a perspective on how AI-driven precision technologies can support a paradigm shift toward agroecological weed management by enabling species-specific interventions that suppress highly competitive weeds while conserving ecologically facilitative or neutral plant communities. Collectively, these advances position AI-enabled precision weed management for reducing chemical inputs, diversifying selection pressure, enhancing agroecosystem resilience, and supporting sustainable agricultural intensification.

papers.title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions
papers.authors: Ziheng Wu, Adrian Vecina Tercero, Andre A. Fatehi, Abhik Sarkar, Brian Giera, Eric B. Duoss, Christopher M. Spadaccini, Nikhil Deshpande, et al.
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific research by integrating robotics, automated experimentation, and machine learning to execute experiments autonomously. Biology and chemistry have adopted these systems. However, increasing SDL complexity heightens susceptibility to unexpected faults in automated workflows, highlighting the need for efficient recovery mechanisms. In this study, we investigate telerobotic interventions to enhance SDL resilience against unexpected failures. We developed a teleoperation interface enabling human operators to resolve disruptions during automated tasks. The interface enables precise control of a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm (UR3e) using a 3D mouse (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro). Two velocity-based controller strategies were evaluated: (i) a coupled mode mapping all six DOFs to the 3D mouse's central knob and (ii) a decoupled mode separating translational and rotational motions. To evaluate the framework, teleoperators intervened across three SDL fault scenarios. In the first study, comparative trials showed that the decoupled controller was associated with shorter completion times and reduced rotational motion. In a second study, teleoperators performed an aiming task with and without reference-path guidance. Users were more target-driven and risk-tolerant without guidance but showed behavioral differences under different guidance strategies. These findings suggest that controller configuration and reference-path design influence operator performance during SDL fault recovery, informing teleoperation interface optimization. This work demonstrates the potential feasibility of teleoperation as a human-in-the-loop recovery mechanism for SDL workflows, combining robotic precision with human adaptability and problem-solving. These findings also provide a foundation for future studies in shared autonomy and semi-autonomous intervention.
