papers.title: From World Foundation Models to Real-world applications: An Introduction
papers.authors: Johan Barthélemy, Dikai Liu, Frank Yunqing Guan, Tomasz Piotr Bednarz
papers.abstract: This course introduces the emerging paradigm of world foundation models (WFMs) and their role in enabling real-world physical AI systems. Those WFMs learn structured, multimodal representations of physical environments, supporting perception, prediction, and decision-making from a shared representation that spans vision, language, and action. The course connects foundation model concepts to dynamic visual environments, simulation, synthetic data generation, robotics, and sim-to-real deployment.

papers.title: From Foundation VLM to Versatile Driving VLM: A Triplet Incremental Training Approach
papers.authors: Shengtao Wu, Zichao Dong, Weixuan Qiao, Xiaolu Liu, Xin Zhan, Junbo Chen, Jianke Zhu
papers.abstract: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.

papers.title: FORGE: Force-Aware Multi-Granularity Control for Efficient Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Liangjun Xing, Ke Fan, Kailin Li, Bin Wang, Xiaojie Niu, Qingwei Ben, Jiafei Cao, Wei Yao, et al.
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion, balance regulation, and manipulation under frequent contacts, making teleoperated demonstration collection difficult: a practical controller must simultaneously provide precision, stability, and contact awareness. We propose FORGE, a force-aware multi-granularity control system with a coarse-to-fine command space spanning velocity navigation, planar foot placement, wrist-pose tracking, and optional force-conditioning inputs. Policy training requires no full-body human motion trajectories or joint-angle references; deployment consumes only sparse bilateral wrist poses relative to the pelvis, coarse motion commands, and optional desired wrist-load inputs. For sustained contact, FORGE combines a momentum observer with a learned correction trained using simulator contact-force supervision. At deployment, it estimates low-frequency, wrist-equivalent interaction forces from proprioception and reconstructed low-level arm PD torques, without wrist force/torque sensors. A quasi-static virtual-target loop uses this estimate and an optional desired applied-force input to adapt the wrist target. A frozen locomotion prior and asymmetric residual actions stabilize manipulation-induced whole-body corrections. Experiments evaluate unified-control stability, task-space tracking, quasi-static wrist-equivalent force estimation, squeezing forces during sustained contact with a rigid box, and downstream diffusion-policy execution of a squat-and-lift task across payload conditions. papers.title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
papers.authors: Yaru Niu, Binghong Chen, Changwei Yao, Shangtao Li, Zhenlong Fang, Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Shuai Zhou, Yuemin Mao, et al.
papers.abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

papers.title: Developing and testing an operational workflow for underwater robotic recovery of abandoned, lost, or otherwise discarded fishing nets
papers.authors: Kristine Cerbule, Armands Šenfelds, Astrīda Rijkure, Mihails Gorobecs, Andrejs Potapovs, Andrejs Stupāns, Jurijs Timofejevs, Pāvels Maksimkins
papers.abstract: Abandoned, lost or otherwise discarded fishing gear (ALDFG) has a potential to adversely affect marine fauna and ecosystems, entangling and killing numerous species and causing marine pollution. Traditional ALDFG removal methods, often including diving or creeping, are labour-intensive, time-consuming, costly, and, in the case of diving, may be hazardous due to poor visibility, low temperatures, strong currents, and dangers of entanglement. Deployment of underwater robotic systems equipped with camera-assisted manipulators presents a promising solution to complement or replace ALDFG retrieval that is relying on diving operations. The development of such systems requires focused research into advanced technologies for underwater mapping, object detection and manipulation for ALDFG retrieval. The aim of this study is to develop and test a system concept, requirements, and a perception-and-control approach for an underwater remotely operated vehicle with manipulators that can locate, assess, and remove ALDFG and other entangling debris. The developed concept was tested in controlled experiments simulating ALDFG retrieval in shallow waters. The results provide a foundation for safe and efficient robotic intervention in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Coordination without command: active inference and the route to embodied intelligence
papers.authors: Alexander D. Shaw
papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence depends on bodies whose contact with the environment, distribution of load and capacity for action are only partly known and are changed by movement. We argue that this creates a practical reason to organize inference through distributed, hierarchical and plural processes, using active inference to relate local belief updating, contextual constraints and action selection within a common framework. The proposal brings together established ideas from factorized inference, distributed control and embodied robotics, distinguishing their mathematical description from the location of computation and authority over action. The octopus provides biological motivation through its combination of peripheral sensorimotor processing and central influences on behavior, while an articulated hexapod illustrates selected architectural choices through six leg-local predictive controllers coupled by neighbor messages and a shared mechanical body. The simulation includes intact locomotion and movement following programmed limb withdrawal and graph reconfiguration, although these observations do not isolate the contribution of inference or establish remapping. Together, the biological example and computational illustration clarify how local inferential processes may remain coordinated across bodily interfaces and timescales without a controller prescribing the complete joint trajectory.

papers.title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents
papers.authors: Jieqiang Wei, Fahad Ali, Jonny Reichwald, Silun Zhang
papers.abstract: LLM agents, i.e., language models run by a harness, can now write, run and debug software autonomously. This raises the question of whether they can also carry out control system design. In this paper, we consider control system design as a task for LLM agents and grade the designed controller as control engineers do: the controller is given in a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, evaluated on held-out seeds against an ordered set of requirements, under specified physical perturbations and structural certificates, without using neural networks. We formulate the task as a chance-constrained feasibility problem and instantiate it in ControlHarbor, a benchmark of 44 tasks over 13 plants, which includes network consensus, vehicle platooning, the MuJoCo hopper, walker and humanoid. The tasks are packaged in the Harbor format, so that any agent harness can be run against them, and the same environments also serve learning algorithms other than LLMs, such as reinforcement learning (RL), under the same evaluation. With ControlHarbor, we observe that the controllers designed by three frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5, reach the RL return on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions. We also observe that the controllers certified for return alone usually fail under perturbations. When robustness is part of the specification, a structured design meets it at the RL return on the humanoid task, where domain-randomised RL does not; under large pushes, domain-randomised RL succeeds and no designed controller does. The benchmark, the controllers, and their grades are released.

papers.title: Collaborative Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems Through Iterative Clustering
papers.authors: David R. Martin, Brooks A. Butler, Scott Nivison, Magnus Egerstedt, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar
papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems face the challenge of efficiently allocating teams of heterogeneous robots to tasks. The task allocation problem is complicated by collaborative interactions between robots where teams of robots develop emergent capabilities that enable them to complete tasks that would be inefficient or impossible for individual robots. To address these challenges, we present an iterative clustering algorithm for collaborative task allocation in heterogeneous multi-robot systems. This approach partitions the computationally intractable global optimization problem into smaller, tractable subproblems by iteratively forming clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizing assignments within each cluster. By ensuring robots remain clustered with their currently assigned tasks, we guarantee monotonic improvement in overall utility with each iteration. We analyze the convergence of the algorithm and characterize how cluster size constraints determine which suboptimal assignments could trap the algorithm. In simulation, iterative clustering consistently outperforms simulated annealing, and a group-based auction in both computation time and solution quality, and outperforms a hedonic game approach in solution quality.

papers.title: BlinkMimic: Training a Humanoid Motion Tracker in Minutes on a Single GPU
papers.authors: Fuyi Chen
papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking lets a humanoid robot follow reference motions, but training a tracking policy for a library of motions has usually taken hours of GPU time. SuperMimic showed that the policy can instead be trained by backpropagating through a world model learned from parallel simulation, and InstantTrack added Muon updates, a residual policy around the reference and an averaged deployed policy. We build on both and present BlinkMimic, a recipe that makes this training faster. On a simulated Unitree G1, BlinkMimic trains one policy for all 40 LAFAN1 clips in 3.4 minutes on a single RTX 4090, measured until three consecutive checkpoints reach a normalized return of at least 0.82 with no failed clip (mean of three seeds). We split training time into the cost of an iteration, the iterations needed to fit the motions, and the iterations needed to remove the last failures, and assign each component, inherited or new, to one of these terms. The new components are a step size that decreases once training has progressed, resets directed by failures of the deployed policy under deployment conditions, and GPU graph capture of the whole iteration. A leave-one-out ablation with three seeds per component shows which term each component affects, and further measurements of the gradient, the update rule and the failure cases explain these effects. Code and per-seed results are available at https://github.com/fuyichen0725/blinkmimic.

papers.title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
papers.authors: BWM Team
papers.abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

papers.title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
papers.authors: Yonghwan Kim, Gil-Tak Kong, Un-Sook Choi
papers.abstract: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

papers.title: AstroMemBench: A Benchmark for Memory Systems in Embodied Spacecraft Agents
papers.authors: You Wu, Guhong Zhang, Hongwei Li, Xinyue Hong, Yuan Jia
papers.abstract: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.

papers.title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning
papers.authors: Pranay Gupta, Deepanshu Rohilla
papers.abstract: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.

papers.title: AgriSense: Vision-Language Decision Support and Robotic Intervention in a Virtual Greenhouse Copy title
papers.authors: Lyes Saad Saoud, Oualid Doukhi, Reza Ghorbani, Moussa Ayyash
papers.abstract: Autonomous greenhouse management increasingly requires robotic systems that integrate perception, navigation, environmental regulation, and plant-level intervention. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework combining an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing, environmental control, and supervised vision-language decision support. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, together with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone, and an intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds on a source-grouped test set, the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations each achieve 43/44 correct zone decisions, providing no evidence of incremental multimodal zone-accuracy improvement. The full model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.249 degrees C for temperature, 2.030 percentage points for humidity, and 0.997 percentage points for soil moisture. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, while language-only inputs achieve 68.64%. External real-image benchmarks reveal distribution-shift limitations. Five offline Point-LIO routes yield rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22-17.32 mm. Of 40 virtual-arm targets, 32 satisfy geometric acceptance criteria and eight are rejected at boundaries. Six long-horizon climate cases and fault protocols characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment rely on simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse performance and agronomic treatment efficacy remain unvalidated. The contribution is an evaluated decision-support and robotic-intervention framework for a virtual greenhouse.

papers.title: Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training
papers.authors: Gongyue Teng, Yuqing Xie, Yixian Zhang, Feng Gao, Shu'ang Yu, Jiaji Rao, Sukai Wang, Guanghui Ren, et al.
papers.abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $π_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

papers.title: ACE-CaP-0: Real-World Code-as-Policies in the Era of Experience
papers.authors: ACE-CaP Team, Changxu Wei, Yunpeng Qing, Guozheng Ma, Bowen Liu, Zexin He, Yilun Kong, Haoming Gu, et al.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in frontier models have pushed the boundaries of agentic robot control, enabling agents to perform complex robotic tasks through reasoning and interaction. However, repeated calls to these models during execution can substantially increase task completion time. Code as Policies (CaP) offers a route for coding agents to acquire physical skills through experience and retain them in executable programs, allowing the reasoning invested in development to be reused across runs. Developing reliable code policies while limiting the cost of physical experimentation remains a central challenge. We investigate human guidance as a source of priors for feasible actions and simulation as an auxiliary environment for exploring and testing candidate policies. Our findings favor robot demonstrations available on request and simulation used selectively during real-world policy refinement. These findings inform ACE-CaP-0, an agentic recipe that couples policy revision with experience acquisition through Demonstrations on Request and Simulation on Demand. Across eight real-world manipulation tasks spanning alignment, multi-object handling, and bimanual coordination, the resulting frozen programs achieve 92.1\% success (221/240 trials). Mean execution times across tasks range from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. The programs execute with runtime perception and control, without a human or coding agent in the loop. These results highlight CaP's potential to turn experience into reliable, reusable physical skills.

papers.title: A Recipe for Physical Action Model Training
papers.authors: Shaojiang Wang, Geer Yang
papers.abstract: Choosing robot model capacity and demonstration budgets also requires decisions about data composition, representation, optimization, and deployment. We connect these decisions through a common conditional-distribution target. Nested learning oracles give exact risk accounting; local information geometry, conditional mutual information, and empirical convergence provide conditional training prescriptions. Known-target numerical checks expose capacity-data coupling, representation-induced mixture mismatch, and an example where deployment KL increases while negative log-likelihood decreases. An analysis of 206 public PushT trajectories evaluates fixed-feature information-design criteria without fitting a policy. Under asymmetric evaluation targets, the selected allocations reduce this criterion by 4.5-6.2% relative to target matching; balanced targets show no benefit. These results clarify which quantities can support training recommendations and when an apparently favorable predictive metric has a different interpretation.

papers.title: A Coupled Control Barrier Function Approach to Deadlock-Free Multi-Robot Conflict Resolution
papers.authors: Gary Rostomyan, Ketan Savla, Petros A. Ioannou
papers.abstract: Many robotic applications involve scenarios where multiple robots interact and the decisions of one robot influence the behavior of others. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based feedback controller for multi-robot conflict resolution with input constraints. Safety is enforced using coupled Control Barrier Function (CBF), while a yielding matrix encodes how robots influence each other. Unlike existing methods with fixed or hard priorities, the proposed framework enables yielding preferences while guaranteeing deadlock-free operation by design. Sufficient conditions are established for the controller to be locally Lipschitz. The optimal CBF sign- indefinite slack is shown to admit a finite uniform bound, which is compensated through an enlarged CBF safety margin to obtain a forward invariant set contained within the desired safe set. The analysis also identifies an irreducible slack component due to finite maximum deceleration that cannot be eliminated by increasing the slack penalty. Finally, sufficient conditions on the yielding matrix and nominal controller are derived to exclude deadlock states. Simulations demonstrate adaptive coordination across yielding preferences and robustness to robot failures.

papers.title: 3D Scene Graphs: Open Challenges and Future Directions
papers.authors: Dennis Rotondi, Francesco Argenziano, Sebastian Koch, Nathan Hughes, Martin Büchner, Johanna Wald, Lukas Rosenberger Schmid, Daniele Nardi
papers.abstract: 3D scene graphs (3DSGs) have emerged as a powerful representation for spatial AI by combining geometric grounding with semantic and relational abstractions of the environment. Their expressiveness has made them relevant to a broad range of problems in robotics and computer vision, including manipulation, navigation, task planning, scene understanding, and many others. However, the field remains fragmented: Different communities adopt distinct formulations, construction pipelines, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to compare methods, identify common assumptions, and assess remaining challenges for robust real-world deployment. This survey provides a unified and critical review of 3DSGs, with particular emphasis on open challenges and future directions. We first formalize 3DSGs under a common definition and analyze the principal modeling choices that characterize existing formulations, including node and edge attributes, hierarchical structure, dynamic scene representations, and affordance-aware extensions. We then review how 3DSGs are built from raw sensory observations, discussing the most common terminologies, conventions, and techniques. Finally, we examine downstream applications and evaluation strategies, from intrinsic graph quality to task-level performance. To support the community, we also provide a dedicated website that organizes and extends the surveyed content, accessible at https://3dscenegraphs.com .

papers.title: ‘KÖNNTEN SIE MIR ERKLÄREN, WAS DARAN LUSTIG IST?’: HUMOUR, INCONVENIENCE AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MARIA SCHRADER'S ICH BIN DEIN MENSCH (2021)
papers.authors: Muriel Cormican
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Through the strategic use of humour, Ich bin dein Mensch poses implicit questions about how we police the boundaries of the human. Recounting the experiences of the protagonist, Alma, with a humanoid robot, Tom — whose humanness she is tasked with evaluating — the film documents and reflects crucial facets of the struggle with unsettled boundaries between the human and non‐human. It evokes affective (laughter/sadness/discomfort) and cognitive (intellectual) responses that invite viewers to think and feel their way through contemporary structures of inequity that are underwritten by the tacit agreement that some are more human than others. The film quietly reveals how the category of human gets constructed and deployed in general, not just in relation to emerging technological threats. Thus, the questions of the film are not really whether Tom should be considered human, or whether there are differences between a human being and embodied artificial intelligence. Rather, Tom functions as a figure through which discourses of superiority, privilege and human rights can be scrutinised.

papers.title: space-robot-dq: a Python library for dual quaternion kinematics, dynamics, and control of free-floating space robot manipulators
papers.authors: Hadi Jahanshahi, Zheng H. Zhu
papers.abstract: This article presents space-robot-dq, an open-source Python library for the kinematics, dynamics, and resolved-rate control of free-floating space robot manipulators using dual quaternion algebra. Unlike ground-based robots, space manipulators operate on platforms with no fixed base. When the arm moves, the spacecraft reacts to conserve momentum, changing the mapping between joint motion and end-effector motion. The library implements Product of Exponentials forward kinematics in dual quaternion arithmetic, numerical and analytical Jacobians, optimization-based inverse kinematics, the Umetani–Yoshida generalized Jacobian for momentum-coupled systems, and closed-loop resolved-rate controllers for a momentum-conserving free-floating plant with base pose propagation. It supports arbitrary N -DOF serial chains of revolute joints through a declarative configuration interface. The implementation is verified by 153 unit tests across four robot architectures and a 19-check benchmark suite. Independent validation covers forward-kinematics agreement below 10 –11 m against two reference implementations that share no code with the library and first-order-convergent stationarity of the system’s center of mass, while construction-level consistency checks confirm momentum residuals at the 10 –15 level. Two control studies quantify the practical consequences of the free-floating coupling. In Cartesian tracking of a 0.27 m maneuver, a controller using the fixed-base Jacobian accumulates 26.372 mm root mean square (RMS) error even with feedback, whereas the generalized-Jacobian controller tracks at 0.2512 mm RMS (a 105-fold difference that measures the cost of the model mismatch alone, because both controllers run on the same plant). In a capture-approach scenario, the end-effector maintains a full 6-DOF grasp pose against a client tumbling at 5° per second, holding 0.008429 mm and 0.000581° RMS with the generalized Jacobian versus 4.267 mm and 0.22° with the fixed-base model (506-fold and 379-fold differences attributable to the neglected coupling), while the spacecraft base drifts 2.4°, an attitude cost the library quantifies for mission design. All figures and numbers in this article are reproduced by a single, deterministic script included in the repository.

papers.title: XR serious games for phantom limb pain, neurofunctional recovery, and prosthetic adoption: a systematic review
papers.authors: Muhannad Farhan, Saad Jawaid Khan, Kehinde Quasim Yusuf, Abu Zeeshan Bari, Muhammad Faisal Siddiqui, Maram Ali Alahmadi, Joyce Zhanzi Wang
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To synthesize evidence on Extended Reality (XR) serious games for Phantom Limb Pain (PLP), neurofunctional recovery, embodiment, and adoption following amputation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched up to January 2026. Eligible studies included adults with limb amputation who received XR serious game interventions and reported rehabilitation or user-experience outcomes. Quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Evidence certainty was rated using GRADE across 5 outcome domains. RESULTS: 24 studies met the inclusion criteria. XR interventions showed consistent PLP reduction, with AR-based phantom motor execution systems reporting the largest effect sizes (d = 0.9-1.3) and preliminary evidence of reversal of cortical reorganization. VR exergames improved gait and balance in 2 RCTs. Immersive VR and EMG systems indicated improved object manipulation, performance time, and motor control. Neurofunctional and embodiment outcomes provided mechanistically plausible evidence regarding cortical activity, embodiment, and physiological adaptation. CONCLUSIONS: XR serious games show preliminary benefit in reducing phantom limb pain, improving functional mobility, supporting prosthesis control, and enhancing embodiment after amputation. Evidence linking XR-mediated sensorimotor feedback to cortical adaptation remains exploratory but is supported by neurofunctional findings. Usability and engagement outcomes were positive, although real-world implementation and scalability remain under-researched.

A tactile generator needs a latent space, and we choose one by testing whether a material classifier trained on real GelSight presses still works on encode-decode reconstructions from pretrained image models. On ObjectFolder Real, the classifier loses 6.5 to 9.7 points on reconstructions from three 16x discrete tokenizers and 0.3 points on those from the Stable Diffusion VAE (SD-VAE). The 16x tokenizers again lose far more on Touch and Go and on DIGIT object recognition (YCB-Slide). Retraining the classifier on reconstructions, with no new labels, narrows the discrete gap. papers.title: Where is My Mug? Training-Free Framework for Personalized Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Quang Qui-Vinh Nguyen, Hung Nguyen, Rang Nguyen, Khoi Nguyen
papers.abstract: \textbf{Personalized Image Segmentation (PIS)} aims to segment the specific object in a target image that matches a user-provided reference. Unlike category-based segmentation or few-shot segmentation, PIS must discriminate between multiple visually similar instances, a requirement central to deployed applications such as augmented reality, personalized content editing, robotics manipulation, inventory tracking, and fine-grained visual retrieval. We show that the strong numbers reported by existing PIS methods are largely an artifact of single-instance benchmarks: when evaluated on realistic scenes with several same-category look-alikes, prior point-prompt methods collapse, because the correct instance is frequently never surfaced as a prompt. We trace this to a recall bottleneck rather than a mask-quality one, and address it with a training-free, modular system. The pipeline first generates high-recall object proposals using an off-the-shelf class-agnostic detector, then matches each proposal to the reference using foundation-model features (e.g., BLIP-2), and finally refines the selected box with SAM. For robust matching we propose \textbf{top-$K$ Sinkhorn}, a patch-level distance that scores each candidate only on its most confidently matched patches; trimming the Sinkhorn dual potentials recovers the robustness of partial optimal transport at more than $100\times$ lower cost, keeping it inside the per-proposal candidate loop. To evaluate this regime, we introduce \textbf{\datasetname}, a realistic multi-instance benchmark. Across \datasetname, PerSeg, PerMIS, and DAVIS, our system surpasses PerSAM, $\mathrm{P}^2\mathrm{SAM}$, and PDM by up to $\sim\!48$ mIoU while matching their runtime and using fewer parameters, establishing a strong, deployable training-free baseline for real-world personalized segmentation.

papers.title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
papers.authors: Kyeongryeol Go
papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.

papers.title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
papers.authors: Zhuoyue Li, Zhendong Han, Pankhuri Vanjani, Wenting Li, Rudolf Lioutikov
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.

papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components. Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation. Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor. We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data. We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training. FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories. We train our policy by joint video-action training. Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches pi_{0.5}'s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform. On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.

papers.title: TyphoonWorld: A Residual Token World Model for Probabilistic Forecasting of Typhoon Imagery
papers.authors: Xiaoyu Chen, Tianyi Li, Xuanyi Zhang
papers.abstract: A satellite forecast of a typhoon should give a low-error picture of the next two days, together with an ensemble whose members are coherent fields and whose spread responds to the storm at hand. A small direct regression network already gives the lowest squared error on held-out storms, so a generative model has to earn its cost through the part of the future that the regression smooths away. We present TyphoonWorld, a discrete-token world model that generates only that part. Conditioned on tokens of the regression forecast, the latest frames and the best-track state at forecast time, it samples residual fields lead by lead, and members add these residuals to the regression center. We compare it under one protocol with per-pixel Gaussian networks, a diffusion model of the same residuals, residuals from other storms and an unconditional token world model, on 276 forecast windows from 46 held-out storms of Digital Typhoon. TyphoonWorld matches the squared error of the regression, lowers the CRPS of the area colder than 220 K, a direct measure of deep convection, by 14 to 39% against every other ensemble, and ties its spread to forecast error as closely as the Gaussian network, with a correlation of 0.78 across windows. It uses 56% of the parameters of the unconditional world model.

papers.title: Topology-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Egocentric Videos
papers.authors: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.

papers.title: The centriole as a fourth counter of replicative aging: a systems analysis of ARGUS, an open autonomous platform for lineage-scale surveillance
papers.authors: Ming Yao
papers.abstract: Replicative aging in dividing cells is commonly described through three resettable counters: telomere length, mitochondrial state, and chromatin organisation. We argue for a fourth: the centriole, a conserved microtubule-based organelle that every animal cell either keeps or eliminates. Three lines of evidence motivate the proposal. First, centriole fate is highly stereotyped: in Caenorhabditis elegans about 88% of somatic cells eliminate their centrioles during embryogenesis, and elimination is coupled to cell fate (Kalbfuss & Gönczy, 2023a). Second, centriole age measurably biases division geometry and cell fate in human cells, including asymmetric inheritance in stem cells (Thomas & Meraldi, 2024; Izumi et al., 2026). Third, unlike telomeres, mitochondria, and chromatin, the centriole has no known disposal-and-reassembly pathway in somatic cells, yet nature performs an analogous reset between meiosis I and the first blastomeres, at the cost of haploidization (Pierron et al., 2023). We present a systems analysis of ARGUS, an open, autonomous, low-cost fluorescence platform for lineage-scale surveillance of centrioles in living specimens, and of its four operating subsystems (OS1–OS4). The subsystems form an epistemic ladder. OS1 asks whether division geometry, summarised as a pre-registered Pedigree Score, predicts centriole fate (correlation). OS2 asks whether pedigree predicts convergence of fate across different lineages (prediction). OS3 tests causality through laser ablation (necessity) and centriole transplantation (sufficiency), and asks whether centriole elimination followed by de novo synthesis can reset cellular entropy without haploidization. OS4 adds inverted-geometry high-numerical-aperture imaging and contact-free optoelectronic-tweezer manipulation. Each stage carries pre-registered, falsifiable criteria and explicit go/no-go gates. We analyse the epistemic structure of the system, its failure modes, and its generalisability, and discuss what a testable fourth counter implies for aging biology and for open, autonomous biological instrumentation.

papers.title: The Posterior-Prior Epistemic Gap: When World Model Imagination Fails to Carry Task-Relevant Signals
papers.authors: Jaerock Kwon, Elahe Delavari, Donghyun Kim, Haewoon Nam
papers.abstract: Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals---a property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator, we identify a \textbf{posterior-prior gap}---posterior (observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay (AUC 0.85$\rightarrow$0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops 57\%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the transition model---not the representation---as the information bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0\% without privileged runtime coordinates, and the planner's own ensemble-based epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning time. As a secondary contribution, we show that \textbf{task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components} over the same world model yields lane keeping ($81.2 \pm 1.8$\% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, \emph{using privileged coordinates}) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.

papers.title: The Physical Grounding Fault: Why Software Audit Sidecars Fail in Embodied Agents
papers.authors: zhizhi(廖至智) liao
papers.abstract: False completion in large language model (LLM) software agents can be audited, in the digital regime, by a four-valued verdict and a software sidecar that records whether a claimed effect was delivered [8]. The same pattern does not transfer to embodied agents. A software exception can roll back a file write; it cannot roll back a crash. Harness-written records are not evidentiary [5]. Vision–language–action (VLA) stacks collapse modular contracts into a stochastic control surface [6]. Independent hardware can take refusal off the host for access governance [2]. None of these results, taken alone, is a theorem about the sidecar. This paper treats the software audit sidecar itself as the failing object. We formalise three structural faults of physical grounding. Fault I (shared-scheduler refusal): when the sidecar shares the controller’s scheduler and fault domain, refusal remains an exception and is unreachable on a physical timescale; NVIDIA Sentry shows that leaving the host is feasible, but does not show that a co-scheduled sidecar is a Simplex shield. Fault II (physical-oracle substitution): the physical world is nearly a free outcome oracle [11], yet the sidecar replaces that oracle with a homologous shadow (logs, self-reports, hashes), so temporal witness is colluded away. Fault III (assurance-coverage collapse): a Lean 4 development can close the discrete four-valued lattice, while worst-case execution time (WCET), allocation freedom, interrupts, and sensor timing drive the fraction of discharged physical objectives toward zero—a collapse of coverage, not of the VLA module graph. Prior work established the ingredients. This paper supplies the unified critique: a sidecar that already works for digital agents fails structurally once the effect is a state of a body. The architecture that remains is a split between a slow record layer and a fast enable layer whose default, on silence, is a predetermined safe state. The discussion is restricted to civil special-use robots and unmanned aircraft (inspection, firefighting, logistics). It is not a first discovery of watchdogs or of stack collapse; it is a unified framework and formal critique of sidecar failure on a physical timescale.

papers.title: TPACK-XD: Expanding the TPACK Framework for Metaverse-Based Higher Education Learning Environments
papers.authors: Cristina Obae
papers.abstract: The integration of immersive metaverse-based environments into higher education challenges existing conceptualisations of teacher knowledge. While the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework has guided technology integration in traditional and online settings, its sufficiency for immersive higher education metaverse-based learning environments (HEMLE) remains underexplored. Grounded in a design-based research (DBR) problem-analysis phase, this qualitative study draws on expert interviews with immersive education practitioners and platform developers to identify the knowledge domains required for effective curriculum design in HEMLE contexts. Using a hybrid thematic analysis informed by TPACK, findings reveal that immersive teaching demands expanded attention to Learner Knowledge (AK), Design Knowledge (DK), and strengthened Contextual Knowledge (XK), reflecting embodied interaction, experiential orchestration, and infrastructural constraints unique to immersive environments. Based on these insights, the study proposes TPACK-XD as an extended framework that accounts for the design-intensive, contextually embedded, and learner-centered nature of metaverse-based higher education. The findings contribute to the theoretical refinement of teacher knowledge models and offer guidance for curriculum development in immersive digital learning spaces.

papers.title: Slip Detection for Robotic Grasping with LSTM and TCN: Edge AI Evaluation on Embedded Platforms
papers.authors: Mohammad Haziq Khan, Mario Radke, Majd Hanna, Raza Saeed, Mingyu Fan, Hongbing Liu, Matthias Rätsch
papers.abstract: Abstract Reliable object grasping is essential for robotic manipulation in real-world environments, such as manufacturing and assembly. Undetected slips can lead to task failure, while effective slip detection enables robots to adapt their grip in real time, improving robustness and safety. In earlier work, we showed that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be deployed on edge devices for real-time slip detection, but that study used a manually labelled dataset and reported only accuracy and F 1 scores, which limited comparisons of model–hardware combinations. In this work, we collect a large slip detection dataset using a Fin Ray-inspired soft gripper with tactile Force Sensing Linear Potentiometers (FSLPs), a Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensor, and an encoder, to generate slip and no-slip labels from automatically estimated ArUco marker poses. We design and evaluate lightweight LSTM and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) architectures trained on sensor sequences and compare their performance on a held-out test set. We then deploy the selected models on several embedded platforms, including Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin, Google Coral Dev Board Micro, ESP32, and Arduino Nicla Sense ME, and benchmark accuracy, F 1 score, average inference time, and estimated average energy per inference. The results show that accurate slip detection is feasible even on constrained microcontroller- class hardware, and provide a more comprehensive comparison of model and hardware choices than previous work.

papers.title: Single-View RGB-D Force--Deformation Estimation for Robotic Manipulation of Elasto-Plastic Materials
papers.authors: Dezhi Sun, Marijn van Hilten, Kenan Niu
papers.abstract: Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes. We investigate the force--deformation relationship using a standard robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates. A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume. Force--volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on 52 force--volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and $R^2=0.440$. A separate comparison shows lower error for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N. An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward. These results establish a practical measurement basis for deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates and single-view geometry.

papers.title: Simulation and Control of an SO-101 Robotic Arm for Assistive Daily Living Tasks
papers.authors: Chinmaya
papers.abstract: Assistive robotic systems have the potential to improve independence and quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by helping them perform everyday tasks. In this article, I investigate the feasibility of using low-cost robotic arms to assist wheelchair users with object manipulation and retrieval. I first assembled and calibrated a physical SO-101 robotic arm system consisting of a leader and follower arm, each with six degrees of freedom. The follower arm was configured to replicate the leader's movements through teleoperation. I then implemented the SO-101 arm in the MuJoCo physics simulation environment and trained it to perform object manipulation tasks, including reaching, grasping, and lifting objects. Building on this work, I developed a simulated assistive wheelchair equipped with two SO-101 robotic arms mounted beside the armrests, providing a framework for exploring coordinated robotic assistance. The proposed system could eventually help wheelchair users retrieve dropped objects, pick up drinking bottles, handle medication containers, and access everyday items without caregiver assistance. This article establishes an initial framework for integrating affordable robotic manipulators with mobility devices, with future work focusing on coordinated dual-arm manipulation, autonomous object detection, and real-world implementation.

papers.title: SIMPLE-C: Multi-LiDAR Extrinsic Calibration using a Simple Moving Reflective Target in Feature-Sparse Maritime Environments
papers.authors: Tim Rehbronn, Max Viehl, Heike Vallery, Tim Reuscher
papers.abstract: Abstract Multi-LiDAR sensor configurations enhance perception for autonomous tasks in robotics compared to single sensors, but they require precise extrinsic calibration. Existing methods often depend on moving the platform or feature-rich environments, making them impractical in extremely sparse maritime settings where water surfaces yield unreliable LiDAR returns and vessels are expensive to move. This paper presents a practical tool for extrinsic online calibration of multiple synchronized LiDARs in such environments called SIMPLE-C (alibration). Our pragmatic approach detects a highly reflective target by combining intensity threshold and spatial clustering with backtracking and filtering. Singular Value Decomposition solves the extrinsics for closed-form point cloud registration. This enables calibration with arbitrary reflective objects like plastic lids with reflective tape or even conventional warning vests within the overlapping field of view. Adaptive outlier rejection and calibration weights enhance robustness. Our approach operates in real time and is quasi-invariant to target dimension or shape, and does not require target-specific geometric calculations, manual transformation inputs or additional sensors. Experiments demonstrate a pairwise calibration accuracy of 5 cm translational and $$0.3^{\circ }$$ 0 . 3 ∘ rotational Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) averaged on sparse water scenarios. On land-based scenarios, we achieve translational accuracy of 3 cm (RMSE). A comparison with state-of-the-art methods, including ICP variants, GMMCalib, CROON, and Fast Global Registration, consistently yields superior results improving translational error by up to 47 % specifically on the water side while achieving similar rotational errors. papers.title: Runtime Safety and Emergency Stops on a Full-Size Humanoid: Deployment Lessons and a Case for Graduated Force Authority
papers.authors: Max Conway, Yutong Zhang, Allen Devaraj, William Xie, Alessandro Roncone, Nikolaus Correll
papers.abstract: Full-size humanoid robots are being considered for hazardous industrial work such as disassembling electric-vehicle batteries. We describe the safety mechanisms of an open-source autonomy stack for the Unitree H1-2 humanoid and what deploying them taught us. All joint commands pass through a safety layer that runs separately from the control software. It enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits, and it stops the robot when a state estimate becomes stale or when the hard-wired emergency stop (e-stop) is pressed or disconnected. We pushed the standing robot until it lost balance. With a model-predictive lower-body controller it never recovered, and the operator had to press the e-stop in every trial. Pressing it removes balance control, and the robot falls. The safety layer's own limits trigger the same stop, and limits chosen for manipulation were exceeded during normal walking. Near an operator or a battery pack, the fall can be more dangerous than the cause of the stop. Joint limits bound how much force a robot can apply, but not when applying it is appropriate. Drawing on research on responsibility and on child and adolescent development, we therefore make a case for granting robots force authority in stages, with a person or organization explicitly responsible for its use.

papers.title: Robot-Induced Bias in Movement Smoothness Metrics for Rehabilitation: Quantification and Correction in Simulation
papers.authors: David Regev, Alex Scherbakov, Eran Beeri Bamani
papers.abstract: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.

papers.title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
papers.authors: Vahid Haratian, Vahid Ansari, Mohammadhossein Malmir, Alois Knoll
papers.abstract: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.

papers.title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
papers.authors: Miao Pan, Kaixiang Yao, Xiaohe Zhou, Xu Wang, Qinfeng Li, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.

papers.title: Reading the Table: Sim-to-Real Game State Detection for the Chef's Hat Card Game
papers.authors: Connor Gäde, Matthias Kerzel, Hauke Bünning, Jan-Gerrit Habekost, Mariana Barros, Stefan Wermter
papers.abstract: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state. When evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot, our pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment, thus providing the perceptual foundation for a robot that can autonomously play Chef's Hat against human players.

papers.title: RUMI: A Robotiq-Matched Universal Manipulation Interface for Robot Learning with Augmented Reality and Haptic Feedback

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.

papers.title: RSLiveBench-UAV: A Continually Evolving Vision-Language Benchmark for Aerial Spatial Intelligence
papers.authors: Yue Zhou, Jiawei Liu, Jue Chen, Ziyang Gong, Haojia Wei, Jingxiang Li, Xue Jiang, Zhihang Zhong, et al.
papers.abstract: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. papers.title: Prediction-Error-Tightened MPC for Socially Compliant Crowd Navigation
papers.authors: Alessandro Febbraro, Federico Rollo, Marcello Farina, Luca Bascetta, Navvab Kashiri
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.

papers.title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
papers.authors: Animesh Maheshwari
papers.abstract: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.

papers.title: PolyMorphWBC: Whole-Body Control from End-Effector Trajectories for Quadrupedal Mobile Manipulation across Arm Morphologies with Extended Reach
papers.authors: Heng Li, Yang Li, Yifan Duan, Ren Fang, Matao Duan, Wenhao Yu, Lu Zhang, Jianmin Ji, et al.
papers.abstract: Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base. At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base. However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology. We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm--base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach. Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion. Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback. We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach. In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30cm position error and 4.81° orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies. In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69--72% and orientation error by 91--97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories. On a physical Go2--ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from pi_0 without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.

papers.title: MiniPose: Miniature-Based Real Data Collection for 6D Pose Estimation of Large Industrial Pipe Segments
papers.authors: Hyunjun Kim, Youngjin Seo, Sungwon Seo, Jiyou Shin, Kunwoo Kim, Chanyong Park, Hyungpil Moon
papers.abstract: 6-DOF pose estimation of large and heavy industrial objects, such as large piping systems in shipyards and structural components in petrochemical plants, remains relatively underexplored in robotic perception. Repeatedly repositioning large objects is physically and spatially demanding, making it difficult to acquire real training data with sufficient pose diversity. Synthetic data offer a scalable alternative, but faithfully reproducing real RGB-D observations, particularly the structured measurement errors of real depth sensors, remains difficult. We propose MiniPose, a practical pipeline for miniature-based real RGB-D data collection that addresses both the data-acquisition burden and the sim-to-real gap. We fabricate a scaled-down replica and capture RGB-D data of it in diverse poses using a real RGB-D camera. RGB images are used directly, while depth maps are converted to a geometrically consistent representation of the full-scale object via a simple inverse scaling transformation. This allows training to incorporate real appearance and sensor measurement characteristics that are difficult to reproduce using synthetic data alone. To examine whether the benefit depends on a particular network, we evaluate two RGB-D pose estimators with different formulations, PVN3D and RDPN6D. Mixing at most 1,000 miniature images per pipe type, less than 10\% of the training data, with 10,000 synthetic images improves the mean ADD-S AUC across pipe types over synthetic-only training for both estimators. A comparison with training on full-scale real data further suggests that miniature data can serve as a proxy where full-scale collection is difficult, reducing the data-collection burden for large industrial objects.
